docs.title: Nordhaven: a GPU cloud partner from hardware handover to first workloads
docs.text:
Nordhaven is a fictional European GPU cloud partner. It has just taken delivery of two pools of rented hardware: an NVIDIA L4 pool in Paris on Scaleway for inference and development, and a 2× H200 SXM5 pool in Finland on Verda for training. This project takes both from bare nodes to their first tenants with NVIDIA's open stack, driven by one Git repository, and records why each piece was chosen over its alternatives.

It's Part 2 of my GPU fleet work. Part 1 built Day 2 operations by hand on a single L4: driver lifecycle from Git, DCGM alerting, a remediation controller I wrote, goodput measurement and a burn-in. Here NVIDIA's own tools take over those jobs, and where Part 1 did the same thing, I compare the two on the same GPU.

Both sites run upstream Kubernetes 1.36 through kubeadm, built by the same bootstrap scripts and synced by ArgoCD from the same repository. The two differences come from the providers: Scaleway's L4 boots with no driver, so the GPU Operator installs one, while Verda's image already ships driver 580.178.04, so the operator runs with its driver component off (ADR 0002). The Finland site sends its metrics to Paris as it runs, so they stay queryable after it's deleted. The architecture page covers every component, the network and the sync order.

docs.title: Reading the rest
docs.text:
• What is simulated: every injected fault, simulated GPU and emulated device, in one list. A GPU doesn't fail on request, so the faults were injected.
  • Decisions: one record per real choice, each with at least two alternatives.
  • Findings: what didn't behave as documented.

Names in commands, labels and outputs keep the project's short prefix and site codes: eu1-fin-gpu-01 is the Finland H200 node, par and fin are the Paris and Finland sites, and eu1.io/pool=gpu is a node label. Renaming them would mean redeploying both sites for no technical gain.

docs.title: Day 0: which versions go together, per hardware class
docs.text:
The use case

In Part 1 I pinned every version of the GPU stack by hand (GPU Operator, driver, DCGM, NFD, scheduler, monitoring) and checked each pin against its release notes. NVIDIA's AI Cluster Runtime (AICR) offers the other way: version-locked recipes, tested together, rendered for Argo CD, with a validator that checks a live cluster against them. Here I compare the two on the same stack: I asked AICR for Nordhaven's two GPU pools and set its answer beside what they run.

Ran 20 to 22 October 2026

AICR has no recipe for either pool as it is built: the L4 and kubeadm are unknown to it, and every H200 recipe requires Ubuntu 24.04 where the Finland image is 26.04. So AICR became the reference for the H200 pool, not its installer (ADR 0003). Its drift check missed a version I changed by hand; Argo CD undid the same change in 11 seconds.

docs.title: What AICR v1.1.0 offers Nordhaven
docs.text:
For the training pool, three H200 recipes on Ubuntu resolve: eks, eks with Kubeflow, and k0s. None is ours. k0s is the closest, because it's the only one that leaves the driver to the host as the Finland provider's image does; but its container toolkit points at k0s's containerd, and every one of them insists on Ubuntu 24.04.

For the inference pool there's nothing to compare: AICR rejects l4 as an accelerator and kubeadm as a service outright, and the generic service it offers for self-managed clusters only has a GB300 recipe.

$ make aicr-recipe
...
eks-h200-training      exit=0  aicr recipe --service eks --accelerator h200 --os ubuntu --intent training
eks-h200-kubeflow      exit=0  aicr recipe --service eks --accelerator h200 --os ubuntu --intent training --platform kubeflow
k0s-h200-training      exit=0  aicr recipe --service k0s --accelerator h200 --os ubuntu --intent training
# What we run, or the closest names to it, refused:
kubeadm-h200           exit=2  aicr recipe --service kubeadm --accelerator h200 --os ubuntu --intent training
    [cli] command failed: error=[INVALID_REQUEST] error parsing criteria: [INVALID_REQUEST] invalid service type: kubeadm exitCode=2
generic-h200           exit=2  aicr recipe --service generic --accelerator h200 --os ubuntu --intent training
...

Full output: recipes-summary.txt.

So AICR is Nordhaven's reference for the H200 pool, not its installer, and the L4 keeps Part 1's hand-pinned values. ADR 0003 has the reasoning and the full version table; the short version:

Same as AICR Newer than AICR AICR behind what Nordhaven needs Nordhaven (the Finland pool; NVSentinel runs in Paris) GPU Operator v26.7.2, NFD 0.19.0, NVSentinel v1.28.0 kube-prometheus-stack 91.4.1, driver 580.178.04, KAI v0.18.6 cert-manager 1.20.2 (NVSentinel asks for 1.21), Kubeflow Trainer 2.2.0 (NVCRE needs 2.2.1)

docs.title: The bundle
docs.text: aicr bundle --deployer argocd turns the k0s recipe into eleven Argo CD Applications under an app of apps. I kept it as evidence, untouched and checked against its own checksums (listing), and synced none of it: in Finland it would install a second GPU Operator, NFD and Prometheus beside the ones the base platform runs.

docs.title: Drift: AICR missed it
docs.text:
On 21 October in Paris, with Argo CD paused for the one Application: a snapshot, NVCRE's controller set back from v0.8.0 to v0.7.0 by hand, a second snapshot and aicr diff between them; then Argo CD resumed and a third snapshot (every command with its time).

UTC What happened 10:52:54 Snapshot 1 10:54:02 Argo CD paused for nvcre (skip-reconcile) 10:54:15 kubectl set image to manager:v0.7.0. The new pod crashlooped on unknown flag: --namespace-access-timeout, a flag the v0.8.0 chart passes; the rolling update kept the v0.8.0 pod serving 10:57:37 Snapshot 2 and aicr diff: "DRIFT DETECTED", 16 changes, every one a runtime counter (sysctl, a random UUID, containerd and kubelet memory). The image change isn't among them 10:57:54 Argo CD resumed 10:58:05 v0.8.0 back, 11 seconds later; the v0.7.0 pod gone 10:58:12 Snapshot 3 and aicr diff: 15 changes, again only counters 
$ make aicr-drift SITE=par
[cli] snapshot diff complete: added=0 removed=0 modified=16
CHANGES (0 added, 0 removed, 16 modified)
KIND      PATH                                        BASELINE                              TARGET
----      ----                                        --------                              ------
...
MODIFIED  OS.sysctl./proc/sys/kernel/ns_last_pid      46758                                 51647
MODIFIED  OS.sysctl./proc/sys/kernel/random/uuid      fdc5589e-a70c-4fbd-9b2b-bea2a5fb7e05  15a9f270-204f-40c3-a2ae-da8657512bd6
MODIFIED  SystemD.containerd.service.CPUUsageNSec     161826597000                          183748188000
...
MODIFIED  SystemD.kubelet.service.MemoryPeak          91459584                              98009088

DRIFT DETECTED

Full output: diff-par-20261021T105737Z.txt.

Why it missed the change: AICR's snapshot keeps one name: tag per image's last path segment. An image pinned by digest, as everything in this repository is, has no tag and reads latest, and the two pods were both called manager, so the inventory had one entry for them. A version change on a digest-pinned workload doesn't show, and what does show is buried in counters that change every second.

So on a GitOps cluster aicr diff isn't Nordhaven's drift detector: Argo CD found and undid the same change in 11 seconds. It stays useful for what Git doesn't own, the node's OS, kernel and services, provided someone filters the counters out first. In Paris it couldn't read the kernel configuration at all: the image has no /boot/config-*.

docs.title: Validation of the Finland pool
docs.text:
On 22 October I took a snapshot of the Finland H200 node and ran aicr validate against the k0s H200 training recipe. It never reached the deployment checks. Its readiness pre-flight passed Kubernetes and the OS family, then stopped on the Ubuntu release:

$ make aicr-validate SITE=fin
...
[cli] readiness pre-flight: constraints=3
[cli] readiness constraint passed: name=K8s.server.version expected=>= 1.34 actual=v1.36.5
[cli] readiness constraint passed: name=OS.release.ID expected=ubuntu actual=ubuntu
[cli] command failed: error=[INVALID_REQUEST] readiness check failed: OS.release.VERSION_ID expected 24.04, got 26.04 exitCode=2
aicr validate exit=2 (2 = readiness pre-flight failed)

Full output: validate-fin-20261022T101408Z.log.

That's the refusal I expected, and it's the whole result: AICR can tell Nordhaven that the Finland node isn't the OS it tested, not whether its components match. The version table above, built by hand, is still the comparison. As in Paris, the snapshot couldn't read the kernel configuration (snapshot).

docs.title: What was simulated
docs.text: Nothing. The recipes, the refusals, the bundle and the validation are AICR's real output against the real clusters; the drift was a real image change, made by hand on purpose.

docs.title: What this can't show
docs.text: AICR building a cluster: nothing here was installed from a recipe. And one H200 node is one data point for a recipe meant for fleets.

docs.title: Day 1: no workloads until the node is certified
docs.text:
The use case

A new GPU node joins Nordhaven's training pool with a staging taint, so nothing but its own tests can run on it. NVIDIA's Cluster Readiness Engine (NVCRE) certifies it, a DCGM diagnostic checks the hardware, and a small gate removes the taint only if both passed. Part 1 had burn-in scripts and a runbook; this makes the check a gate in front of tenants.

Ran on the Paris L4 (21 October 2026) and the Finland 2× H200 node (22 October)

The H200 node was certified at 351 GB/s all-reduce bus bandwidth over NVLink and opened to tenants 19 min 39 s after it was Ready, image pull included. One gap showed up that the gate didn't catch at the time: ECC is off on the provider's H200s, so the DCGM diagnostic skipped its memory test and still passed. The gate now refuses that case. Results.

docs.title: The gate
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  join["H200 node joins<br/>taint eu1.io/staging=pending:NoSchedule"] --> cert["NVCRE certification<br/>nccl-all-reduce<br/>nccl-loopback-nvswitch"]
  join --> diag["ECC mode, then dcgmi diag -r 2<br/>as an NVCRE WorkloadRun"]
  cert --> gate["promote.py<br/>every check passed?"]
  diag --> gate
  gate -->|yes| open["taint removed<br/>tenants can schedule"]
  gate -->|no| keep["taint kept<br/>cause: hardware, tooling or unclear"]

The taint goes on at join, through the node's kubeadm JoinConfiguration, so there's no moment when the node is schedulable before it's checked. The GPU Operator's operands and NFD tolerate it, since the node is useless until they run. NVCRE injects the same toleration into its own workload pods through taintSelectors, and its run only targets nodes that still carry the taint. NVCRE itself never taints, cordons or labels a node (its README says so), so promotion is mine: promote.py reads NVCRE's results file, the diagnostic log and the raw NCCL log, and says yes only when everything passed.

When it says no, it also says why, because what happens next depends on it. A hardware failure means no tenant goes on that node. A tooling failure (the run didn't finish, an image couldn't start) allows a manual override, recorded and labelled eu1.io/certification=overridden. Anything in between, for example NCCL leaving NVLink inside one node while the diagnostic is clean, or a diagnostic test that was skipped, goes to a person to decide.

docs.title: What NVCRE needed on this hardware
docs.text:
Read in the source and docs at v0.8.0, and checked by rendering the runs offline with nvcrectl:

NVCRE default On Nordhaven's nodes Set to An H200 node has 8 GPUs The Finland instance, 2H200.141S.88V, is a two-GPU slice of an HGX board; the run finds no node able to supply 8 and fails gpusPerNode: 2 The L4 isn't in the catalog It falls back to 4 GPUs per node, with a warning gpusPerNode: 1 No thresholds PASSED only means the test ran A bus bandwidth floor in Finland (below) Only DCGM category: level 4 Hardcoded --run 4, about 90 minutes on healthy hardware dcgmi diag -r 2 beside the certification Controller "needs a node without GPUs" The docs say so, the chart doesn't enforce it A required node affinity on nvidia.com/gpu.present DoesNotExist nccl-loopback Disables P2P and shared memory, so it tests the network path, not NVLink nccl-loopback-nvswitch, the variant that keeps P2P on

docs.title: The threshold, and where it comes from
docs.text:
No published figure gives the all-reduce bus bandwidth of two H200s in one node, and I won't invent one. What I can say from NVIDIA's H200 page is that PCIe Gen5 carries 128 GB/s in total, 64 GB/s each way, and NVLink 900 GB/s, about 450 each way. So the floor is 64 GB/s: above it, the traffic can only have crossed NVLink. It proves the path, not the performance, and I report the measured figure against 450.

The NCCL log is kept raw, with NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, so the transport each channel used is on record too.

docs.title: The image and the driver
docs.text: NVCRE runs its NCCL tests in nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:26.01-py3, built for driver 590.48.01 (CUDA 13.1.1). The Finland provider's image ships driver 580.178.04. I kept pytorch:25.11-py3, built for 580, as a fallback, after checking its layers for the two binaries the test calls: /usr/local/bin/all_reduce_perf_mpi, and mpirun through /usr/local/mpi, a link to HPC-X. It wasn't needed (below). Both images are pinned by digest.

docs.title: The H200 node, from Ready to open
docs.text:
On 22 October the Finland GPU node joined already carrying eu1.io/staging=pending:NoSchedule. Times are UTC.

Time What happened 09:54:10 Node Ready, tainted; the GPU Operator and NFD start on it 09:55:44 2 GPUs allocatable 09:56:33 to 10:02:07 NVCRE's image (9.1 GB) pulled ahead of the run, 3 min 7 s once its turn came 10:02:42 A separate acceptance test passed (cuda-vectoradd, nvidia-smi), on the same taint toleration 10:03:07 to 10:12:08 NVCRE certification, both categories, one after the other 10:12:41 to 10:12:54 dcgmi diag -r 2 on both GPUs, as an NVCRE WorkloadRun 10:13:49 The gate passed all 7 checks and removed the taint

19 minutes 39 seconds from Ready to open, more than a quarter of it pulling images. Part 1's burn-in took three hours on one L4 and ended with a person running a checklist.

Category Runtime Bus bandwidth (16 GB messages) Against the 64 GB/s floor Against NVLink's ~450 GB/s each way communication/nccl-all-reduce 4 min 31 s 351.45 GB/s 5.5× 78% communication/nccl-loopback-nvswitch 4 min 27 s 351.87 GB/s 5.5× 78%

The summary's Transport: Socket is wrong for this run. "Socket" is the name of NCCL's network plugin for traffic between nodes, which a run inside one node never uses (finding). The raw NCCL log says how the bytes really travelled: NCCL 2.29.2 built a graph of type NVL/PIX, and each run connected 48 channel paths over P2P, via P2P/CUMEM in the two-process all-reduce and via P2P/direct pointer in the single-process loopback, with none over the network. The gate reads those lines, not the summary.

$ grep -E "type NVL/PIX|via P2P" nvcre-fin-20261022T100307Z-nccl.log

The diagnostic's own PCIe test, on the same GPUs, measured 53 to 57 GB/s each way, so the floor sat where it should: just above what PCIe delivers, far below what NVLink did.

The image question resolved itself, though not the same way for both runs. The MPI all-reduce reported cudaDriverVersion 13010: it ran through the image's CUDA forward compatibility libraries. The single-process loopback reported 13000, the host driver's own CUDA 13.0, and ran through CUDA's minor version compatibility. Either way the 25.11 fallback stayed unused.

docs.title: The diagnostic, and the gap in it
docs.text:
dcgmi diag -r 2 passed overall in 13 seconds: the software and PCIe tests passed on both GPUs, and the memory test was skipped on both:

$ dcgmi diag --host nvidia-dcgm.gpu-operator.svc:5555 -r 2 -j
...

                        "results" : 
                        [
                            {
                                "entity_group" : "GPU",
                                "entity_group_id" : 1,
                                "entity_id" : 0,

docs.title: The L4 test of the same gate
docs.text: On 21 October the same gate ran on the Paris L4 with gpusPerNode: 1: staged at 17:23:23 UTC, certified in 1 min 57 s, diagnostic passed in 11 s (software, memory and PCIe, with ECC on), promoted at 17:25:54. The bus bandwidth was 0, as it has to be with one rank, so this proved the plumbing (the taint, the injected toleration, the results file, the log capture, the diagnostic as a WorkloadRun, the gate) and nothing about the L4 (report, gate).

docs.title: What level 2 didn't check
docs.text: Level 2 isn't NVCRE's level 4: no targeted power or targeted stress (20 minutes each), no nvbandwidth, and on the H200 no memory test either. Level 3 would add the longer stress tests; I haven't run it, and its memory test would only run with ECC on.

docs.title: What was simulated
docs.text: Nothing on this page. The node, the GPUs, the NVLink traffic and the diagnostic are all real; the only thing staged by hand is the taint on the Paris L4, which joins the cluster without one (what is simulated, for the whole project).

docs.title: What one node can't show
docs.text: Inter-node fabric: there's one node, so no InfiniBand, RoCE or cross-node NVLink. NVSwitch at rack scale, which NVCRE's multi-node categories exist for. And the training categories, which need at least 4 GPUs (nemotron5-8b) or 32 (nemotron5-56b).

docs.title: Day 2: from a GPU fault back to service, with NVSentinel
docs.text:
The use case

A GPU fails in the middle of a training run. Software should notice, take the node out of service, move the work, repair the node and bring it back, with nobody awake. Part 1 did this with a controller I wrote; here NVIDIA's NVSentinel does it on the same L4, with the same training job and the same injected fault, and I compare the two timelines phase by phase.

Ran on the Paris L4, 21 October 2026

Fault to resumed training in 288.8 seconds against Part 1's 360.9, goodput 73.0% against 66.4%, and no person involved at any step. The time didn't disappear, though: 82% of it is now a reboot and a driver rebuild that Part 1 never did. Results, evidence.

docs.title: Part 1, the number to beat
docs.text:
In Part 1 a simulated XID 79 hit a training job at step 394 and cost it 360.9 seconds of outage; the run finished at 66.4% goodput (918.2 s useful out of 1383 s). Most of that outage wasn't the fault at all:

Phase Seconds What it was Lookback 299.4 A five-minute rule I wrote, because node-problem-detector replays old kernel lines when it restarts Waiting for a person about 40 Nobody had run make return-to-service yet dcgmi diag -r 2 6 The diagnostic that decides whether the GPU can go back Reset and uncordon 12 Restarting node-problem-detector so its condition cleared Restart 3.9 Scheduling, container start, CUDA start

83% of it was my timer and 11% was a human. That's what NVSentinel has to answer: does a maintained, event-driven pipeline remove those two, and what does it cost instead? (Part 1, session D)

docs.title: What NVSentinel does with an XID 79
docs.text:
Read in the source at v1.28.0, before trusting anything else:

flowchart LR
  inj["SIMULATED XID 79<br/>kernel log line"] --> sys["syslog-health-monitor<br/>reads journald every 15 s"]
  sys --> pc["platform-connectors<br/>node condition, MongoDB event"]
  pc --> fq["fault-quarantine<br/>cordon"]
  fq --> nd["node-drainer<br/>evicts through the Eviction API"]
  nd --> fr["fault-remediation<br/>XID 79 = RESTART_BM"]
  fr --> j["janitor<br/>RebootNode"]
  j --> jp["janitor-provider generic<br/>busybox Job: chroot /host reboot"]
  jp --> back["new boot ID, node Ready,<br/>healthy events, uncordon"]
  • The syslog monitor reads the systemd journal, not /dev/kmsg, and matches the NVRM: Xid (PCI:...) pattern in pkg/patterns/xid.go.
  • XID 79 maps to RESTART_BM in NVIDIA's XID catalog, which NVSentinel embeds, so the remediation is a node reboot, not a GPU reset.
  • The node comes back by itself: when the monitors report healthy after the new boot, fault-quarantine uncordons it. Nothing runs a diagnostic first unless post-remediation validation is turned on, and I left it off (see what still isn't automated).

docs.title: What I had to change from the defaults
docs.text:
Each of these would have stopped the run on one GPU node, and each comes from reading the chart at v1.28.0 (nvsentinel-par.yaml):

Default Why it breaks here Set to Drain mode AllowCompletion for every namespace Never evicts: a training job would hold the node until it finished, and remediation would never start Immediate, so the trainer gets the same DisruptionTarget eviction Part 1's Job expects Circuit breaker on (50% of GPU nodes in 5 minutes) With one GPU node the first cordon trips it, and a tripped breaker also blocks the uncordon, with no automatic reset Off in Paris. On a fleet I'd keep it, with an absolute cap (maxCordonedNodes) as well as the percentage janitor-provider.csp.provider: kind Sleeps a few seconds and reports a reboot that never happened generic: a privileged busybox Job that reboots the node MongoDB through Bitnami The Bitnami images are amd64 only, so the values I test on an arm64 laptop wouldn't be the values deployed Percona, one member, on local-path

Part 1's injection needed a change too. Its kernel log line never reaches NVSentinel: a line written to /dev/kmsg from userspace gets logged at LOG_USER, and journald then treats NVRM: as the syslog identifier and strips it from the message, so the pattern can't match. A real XID comes from the kernel and keeps it. I showed this on systemd 255, the version the Paris nodes run (fc2-journald), and the injection now puts the node's uptime in front of NVRM, which is also how NVSentinel's own tests write it. Same write, same moment in the run, one prefix.

docs.title: Checked without a GPU first
docs.text:
Check Result Every chart rendered as Argo CD will, all three stages on Every NVSentinel control pod asks for the CPU pool; no webhook can block core resources while that worker is off; images pinned Server-side dry run against the Paris cluster 177 objects accepted NVSentinel's own KIND demo, on an arm64 Mac Fault, cordon, eviction, RebootNode, recovery The Paris values in KIND, one stage at a time Stage 1 a condition only; stage 2 cordon and drain; stage 3 a RebootNode; NVSentinel uncordoned the node itself each time

KIND couldn't cover three pieces: the syslog monitor, the labeler and a real reboot. The L4 run on 21 October was their first time on real hardware, and all three worked on the first try.

docs.title: How I measure it
docs.text:
The training job, its checkpoints in Garage and the goodput analysis are Part 1's, unchanged, so 66.4% and the new figure mean the same thing. The injection time comes from the L4's own clock, in the same SSH command that writes the line. Everything after it comes from a recorder on my laptop that watches the node, the trainer's pods, the RebootNode objects and the GPU Operator's pods, with the clock offsets between laptop, node and control plane measured at the start.

Phase Ends when Detection NVSentinel's node condition goes True Quarantine The node is cordoned Drain The trainer pod is gone Remediation A RebootNode exists Reboot The node is Ready on a new boot ID Driver The GPU Operator has rebuilt the driver and the GPU is allocatable again Return The node is uncordoned Resume The next attempt starts loading its checkpoint

docs.title: Why the outage is still almost five minutes
docs.text:
The waiting is gone: no timer, no person. What replaced it is work Part 1 skipped. Part 1 treated XID 79 by running a diagnostic and handing the GPU back; NVIDIA's catalog says XID 79 ("GPU has fallen off the bus") needs a reboot, so NVSentinel reboots. On the Paris L4 that costs 238 s: 115 s for the VM to come back and 123 s for the GPU Operator to rebuild the driver, because the operator compiles it on the node at every boot there. A precompiled driver would take most of those 123 s away; that's a trade for the driver decision (ADR 0002), not for this page. On a fleet the job wouldn't wait for any of it: it would restart on another node as soon as the drain finished, about 3 s after the fault.

The kubelet's own events show the same reboot from the node's side, a few seconds behind the API (the cordon was at 17:03:24.8; the kubelet logged it at 17:03:32):

docs.title: The same fault through DCGM
docs.text:
After the measured run I injected XID 79 a second way, into DCGM's cache, with no training running. The DCGM monitor raised GpuAllWatch (DCGM_FR_FALLEN_OFF_BUS) and the node was cordoned 5.7 s after the injection; it was Ready on a new boot 103.8 s later, allocatable 121.4 s after that, and uncordoned 52.4 s after that: 283.3 s in all, within 6 s of the first run (timeline). Both of NVSentinel's detection paths work on the real L4.

Before the measured run, a SIMULATED XID 13, which the catalog marks as needing no action, raised an event 11.8 s after injection and left the node schedulable:

docs.title: What went well, and what didn't
docs.text:
The first real test of three things KIND couldn't show, the syslog monitor, the labeler and a real reboot, passed without a retry, and the [uptime] prefix on the injection did what the journald analysis said it would. The cordon came 1.3 s after the fault, so the fallback I had ready (injecting through DCGM if nothing happened within 2 minutes) was never needed.

Two things nearly got in the way. Scaleway showed no L4 free in either Paris zone a few minutes before the run; one freed up shortly after. And the Paris API server had stalled at 12:07 UTC that day, when Grafana starved etcd's disk, so every NVSentinel, NVCRE and Trainer controller carried 8 to 10 restarts into the run. The restart counts I took before the injection are what show that the run itself caused only two, both on the L4 when it rebooted (before, after).

docs.title: What still isn't automated
docs.text:
The node went back to tenants without a diagnostic. It returned 32 s after the GPU was allocatable, because the monitors said healthy, and nothing ran dcgmi diag first; Part 1's return did. Post-remediation validation (fault-quarantine's validation with lifecycle-manager) would run a DCGM diagnostic for RESTART_BM before the uncordon. I left it off to measure NVSentinel as shipped, and I'd turn it on for tenants: it adds the diagnostic's minutes to every outage, which is cheap next to a tenant landing on a bad GPU.

Two more gaps, both read in the source and not exercised here. An XID the catalog maps to CONTACT_SUPPORT leaves the node cordoned until a person acts. And NVSentinel only protects the L4 while the Paris CPU worker is on, since its control pods live there: with the worker off, a fault would be logged by the monitors on the L4 and nothing would act on it.

docs.title: What was simulated
docs.text: The fault. A healthy GPU can't be made to fall off the bus on request, so every XID on this page was written by a script: XID 79 and XID 13 as kernel log lines, prefixed with the node's uptime, and XID 79 again into DCGM's field cache. Everything after the injection was real: the cordon, the eviction, the reboot of the VM, the driver rebuild, the uncordon and the training job resuming from its checkpoint. (What is simulated, for the whole project.)

docs.title: What one L4 can't show
docs.text: The job can only resume on the node that failed, where a fleet would move it elsewhere and the reboot would cost the job nothing but the reschedule. And a real XID 79 usually kills the process mid-step with a CUDA error, where this trainer gets a clean SIGTERM from the eviction.

docs.title: Use case 4: sharing scarce GPUs between tenants
docs.text:
Nordhaven rents out GPUs that never cover demand, so it has to answer three questions for every tenant: how much is guaranteed, what can be borrowed when others are idle, and what happens to a distributed job that only partly fits. In Part 1 the answer was a ResourceQuota on a time-sliced L4, which capped each tenant and nothing more.

Here the answer is KAI Scheduler v0.18.6 on both sites, with MIG on the Finland H200s. ADR 0006 says why KAI and not Kueue or Volcano, and ADR 0008 says which tenants get MIG, time slicing or whole GPUs.

What ran

On simulated GPUs at the Paris site, on 21 October: borrowing, reclaim and a refused gang, plus a two-pod gang with real containers on the CPU worker. On the Finland H200 node, after it passed certification, on 22 October: the two-pod gang with NCCL, a refused gang of 3, and MIG with two tenants on one H200. One check failed there: KAI won't place a whole-GPU pod next to MIG slices on the same node, which changed ADR 0008.

docs.title: What's built
docs.text:
The same KAI on both sites. One Application per site carries the chart and that site's queues (gitops/apps/{par,fin}/scheduling/kai-scheduler.yaml). Two teams, team-a and team-b, sit under one parent queue with half the GPUs each as quota and no limit:

Queue Paris (simulated) Finland (real) Meaning eu1 8 GPUs 2 GPUs the pool team-a quota 4 quota 1 guaranteed; more can be borrowed while team-b is idle team-b quota 4 quota 1 the same

Only GPUs count against these quotas, with CPU and memory left unlimited; otherwise every pod would sit over quota on CPU, and KAI could always take it back. A workload joins with schedulerName: kai-scheduler and the label kai.scheduler/queue. A Job becomes a gang with one annotation, kai.scheduler/batch-min-member, and KAI's pod grouper creates the PodGroup from it.

Paris: simulated GPUs. Two KWOK nodes, eu1-par-sim-gpu-01 and -02, carry four simulated H200s each from run-ai/fake-gpu-operator 0.2.1. SIMULATED: no VM sits behind them, and a pod bound there shows Running without starting a container. KAI's decisions are real: which pod goes where, whose pods it takes back, and which gang it refuses. The simulated page lists them.

Running the fake operator at the Paris site took two changes from its quick start. Paris already runs the real GPU Operator, which strips the fake operator's nvidia.com/gpu.deploy.* labels from any real node without an NVIDIA PCI device (controllers/nodelabeling_controller.go at v26.7.2), so only the fake operator's KWOK path is installed: there, its device plugin writes nvidia.com/gpu straight into the KWOK node's status, and the labels don't matter. And neither KWOK nor the fake operator lets you set a nodeSelector, so both are vendored (scripts/scheduling/render-sim-gpu.sh) and patched onto the CPU worker, with every image pinned by digest.

One side effect showed up once they joined. Prometheus found a kubelet on each KWOK node, couldn't scrape it, and fired TargetDown and KubeletInstanceUnreachable (capture). The Paris kubelet ServiceMonitor now drops eu1-par-sim-gpu-.*, and both alerts cleared.

Finland: real GPUs and MIG. KAI runs on the Finland CPU node. The GPU Operator overlay enables the MIG manager with a layout of my own, h200-split: GPU0 becomes two 3g.71gb instances, and GPU1 stays whole. Nothing changes until the node carries the label nvidia.com/mig.config=h200-split. A second layout, rtxpro-split, does the same on 2x RTX PRO 6000 (two 2g.48gb instances), for the case where the provider has no H200 free. The H200 run didn't need it.

docs.title: Paris, simulated GPUs: borrowing, reclaim, all or nothing (21 October)
docs.text:
make sched-sim-demo runs three steps, and all passed. Times are UTC.

$ make sched-sim-demo
...
## 1. team-a bursts to 8 GPUs while team-b is idle   [11:27:36Z]
after 5s: 8 team-a pods bound
...
PASS: team-a pods bound, 4 of them over quota (8)
...
## 2. team-b submits a gang of 4; KAI reclaims team-a's borrowed GPUs   [11:27:43Z]
after 5s: team-b's 4 gang pods bound
...
PASS: team-b gang pods bound (4)
PASS: team-a pods still Running (its quota) (4)
...
## 3. team-a done; team-b asks for a gang of 6 with 4 GPUs free   [11:28:02Z]
...
PASS: gang of 6: pods bound (0)
PASS: gang of 6: pods Pending (6)
...
all checks passed

Full capture

  1. Borrowing. team-a asked for 8 single-GPU pods while team-b was idle. All 8 bound within 5 seconds, and the team-a queue showed 8 GPUs allocated against a quota of 4.
  2. Reclaim. team-b submitted a gang of 4 at 11:27:43. At 11:27:46 KAI evicted 4 of team-a's pods, and at 11:27:48 it bound all 4 of team-b's pods in the same second. team-a kept its other 4 pods, and both queues ended at 4 GPUs each: what was borrowed went back, and nothing in quota was touched. KAI's event says "preempted by workload team-b/…"; the pods it picked belonged to a queue running over its quota.
  3. All or nothing. With team-a gone, 4 GPUs were free, and team-b asked for a gang of 6. After 90 seconds none of the 6 had bound, and the 4 free GPUs were still free. KAI's reason on the PodGroup: "Resources were found for 4 pods while 6 are required for gang scheduling." A scheduler without gangs would have bound 4 pods to wait for 2 that never come.

docs.title: Paris, a gang with real containers (21 October)
docs.text: make sched-gang SITE=par runs the same two-pod Job as on the H200s, with gloo instead of NCCL, on the CPU worker. KAI bound both pods at 11:30:06, in the same second, and the all-reduce completed (capture). Its 2.41 GB/s peak says something about one VM's memory and pod network, not about GPUs. The number that mattered later is the image pull: 1 minute 35 seconds for the 4.26 GB trainer image, which is why the Finland node pulls it in advance, as soon as it joins.

The all-reduce between the two pods peaked at 2.24 GB/s of bus bandwidth. Certification measured 351 GB/s on the same two GPUs, inside one pod that sees both, about 157 times more, with every channel over NVLink:

$ grep -m2 "via P2P" docs/artifacts/readiness/nvcre-fin-20261022T100307Z-nccl.log
2026-10-22T10:07:42.817807006Z eu1-fin-h200-communicatio-a82b3-job-workload-node-0-0:1:83 [0] NCCL INFO Channel 00/0 : 0[0] -> 1[1] via P2P/direct pointer

NVCRE's report, its NCCL log, use case 2

NCCL_DEBUG=INFO says why. Each pod reports nNodes 2 localRanks 1, then Using network Socket, and every channel runs via NET/Socket/0 over eth0, the pod network. NCCL treats two pods on one machine as two machines, and NVLink sits unused between them. I expected that, and now it's measured. A tenant whose two-pod gang lands on one node gets a fraction of the interconnect they pay for. The safe fix on a shared platform is to run such a job as one pod holding both GPUs. Opening NVLink between separate pods means giving them more of the host than a multi-tenant platform should hand out by default, and I didn't test it.

Then a gang of 3 on the node's 2 GPUs: after 60 seconds none of the 3 pods had bound. KAI's reason on the PodGroup: "Resources were found for 2 pods while 3 are required for gang scheduling."

Full capture

The MIG manager went to pending within a second and to success 33 seconds later, with no reboot. 44 seconds after that, the device plugin advertised two 3g.71gb instances and nvidia.com/gpu: 1. team-a's and team-b's pods each asked for one instance and got one. Both ran on the same physical H200, on two different MIG devices, and CUDA in each saw 69.8 GiB, not the H200's 141 GB. That's two tenants on one GPU, each with its own memory, compute and fault domain: what Part 1's time slicing on the L4 couldn't give.

The whole-GPU pod didn't run. team-a's third pod asked for nvidia.com/gpu: 1, meant for GPU1, and stayed Pending for 5 minutes although the node advertised that GPU. I resubmitted it alone, with no MIG pod running and team-a well within quota, and KAI refused it again:

$ kubectl -n team-a get podgroups.scheduling.run.ai pg-whole-a-388d847f-caba-4ba1-99a2-7d15c518d67a -o jsonpath='{.status}'
{"resourcesStatus":{"requested":{"nvidia.com/gpu":"1"}},"schedulingConditions":[{"lastTransitionTime":"2026-10-22T10:24:38Z","message":"PodSchedulingErrors: Resources were not found for pod team-a/whole-a due to: no nodes with enough resources were found: 1 node(s) didn't have enough resources: GPUs. \n1 non MIG jobs cant run on a node with MigStrategy='mixed'..","nodePool":"default","reason":"Unschedulable","reasons":[{"message":"Resources were not found for pod team-a/whole-a due to: no nodes with enough resources were found: 1 node(s) didn't have enough resources: GPUs. \n1 non MIG jobs cant run on a node with MigStrategy='mixed'.","reason":"PodSchedulingErrors"}],"status":"True","transitionID":"1","type":"UnschedulableOnNodePool"}]}

Full capture

That's a rule in KAI v0.18.6 (pkg/scheduler/api/node_info/node_info.go): on a MIG-enabled node labelled nvidia.com/mig.strategy=mixed, any task that isn't a MIG request gets a fit error. The GPU Operator's mixed strategy exists to offer whole GPUs and MIG slices side by side on one node. KAI doesn't schedule that way. So with KAI, MIG and whole GPUs split per node, not per GPU. ADR 0008 says so, and it's in the findings.

docs.text:
• Gangs across nodes. The Finland site has one GPU node, so the gang is two pods on one machine. Placement across a rack, and topology-aware scheduling, need more than one node.

docs.title: Use case 5: a Slurm group on the same platform
docs.text:
One of Nordhaven's first customers is a research group that has used Slurm for years. Its people submit with sbatch and srun and won't rewrite their scripts as Kubernetes Jobs. Nordhaven doesn't want a second fleet for them. So Slurm runs inside the Paris Kubernetes cluster through Slinky, SchedMD's own operator, on the same CPU worker, monitoring and health story as every other tenant. ADR 0007 says why Slinky and not Soperator or a separate Slurm cluster.

What ran

Slurm has run at the Paris site since 21 October, and make slurm-test passes all four of its checks. Slurm with GPUs at the Finland site is not built: its design is in its own section.

docs.title: What's built
docs.text:
One Application, slinky (gitops/apps/par/scheduling/slinky.yaml), with four sources: the slurm-operator chart 1.2.3, the slurm chart 1.2.3, the values in gitops/values/scheduling/, and a small bootstrap manifest. Everything runs in the slurm namespace on the Paris CPU worker (eu1.io/pool: cpu), with Slurm 26.05:

Part What it is Notes slurm-operator and its webhook Reconcile Slinky's Controller, NodeSet, LoginSet and RestApi objects One replica each, leader election off (see below). The webhook's certificate comes from cert-manager slurm-controller-0 slurmctld, the Slurm scheduler Its save state sits on a 2 GiB local-path volume, on the worker's disk, so it survives a power-off slurm-worker-cpu-0, -1 slurmd, as Slurm nodes cpu-0 and cpu-1 in partition cpu Both on the one VM (oversubscribeNode), standing in for two machines slurm-login-hpc The login pod where users run sbatch, srun and squeue ClusterIP only slurm-restapi slurmrestd The operator talks to Slurm through it

No accounting: sacct and fair share over time need slurmdbd and a MariaDB, which this PoC doesn't run.

Keys made in the cluster, not in Git. Slurm needs a shared auth key and a JWT key. The slurm chart can create them, but with randAscii and lookup on immutable Secrets, which ArgoCD renders differently on every sync (a finding). So the chart's own key creation is off, and a Job in sync wave -1, slurm-keys-bootstrap, creates slurm-auth-slurm and slurm-auth-jwt once, only if they're missing, as immutable Secrets. At the Paris site it completed at 11:37:32 UTC on 21 October. No key exists in Git or on a laptop, and a sync never rotates one. The namespace's other Secrets are slurm-login-hpc-ssh-host-keys, the two webhook CAs from cert-manager, and slurm-sssd-conf.

A health check before every job. A prolog, 00-node-health.sh in gitops/values/scheduling/slurm.yaml, runs on the Slurm node before each job. It fails if /tmp isn't writable, if less than 256 MiB of memory is available, or if the marker file /var/run/eu1-simulated-fault exists. SIMULATED: the marker is the fault the test creates on purpose (simulated page); the other two checks are real. When the prolog fails, Slurm drains the node and holds the job. It's the Slurm side of use case 2's readiness gate.

How users get in. The test runs commands in the login pod with kubectl exec. No identity provider is wired in (slurm-sssd-conf is empty), so nobody can ssh in. Giving the research group real logins means pointing sssd at their directory and exposing the login Service.

Full capture

  1. The cluster from both sides. The pods and Slinky objects from Kubernetes, then sinfo: partition cpu with cpu-0 and cpu-1 idle, 8 CPUs and about 31 GiB each, both on the same VM.
  2. A user's jobs. srun -N2 -l hostname ran across both nodes. An sbatch job finished COMPLETED in 7 seconds.
  3. The prolog drains a sick node. The test created the simulated fault marker in cpu-0 at 12:16:58 and sent a job there. At 12:16:59 Slurm drained cpu-0 with reason "Prolog error" and held the job (launch_failed_requeued_held). The test then removed the marker, resumed the node and released the job, which completed on cpu-0 with Restarts=1. From the release to COMPLETED took 160 seconds.
  4. Kubernetes drains a Slurm node. The test annotated pod slurm-worker-cpu-1 with nodeset.slinky.slurm.net/pod-cordon=true. Within 6 seconds Slurm showed cpu-1 drained, with the reason "slurm-operator: Pod (slurm/slurm-worker-cpu-1) was cordoned", and the pod carried the condition SlurmNodeStateDrain=True. Removing the annotation brought cpu-1 back to idle within 6 seconds.

The fourth check annotates one pod rather than cordoning the CPU worker, because other workloads share that worker. Cordoning a Kubernetes node goes down the same path in the operator (syncCordon in internal/controller/nodeset/nodeset_sync.go at 1.2.3), but this test doesn't show it.

One gap in the third check: the drain shows in sinfo but not as a condition on the pod. The operator writes pod conditions when it reconciles, and the test reads them within a second of the drain.

docs.title: What went wrong first
docs.text:
The first sync and the first test run turned up four problems. Each one is fixed in Git, and they're worth knowing before installing Slinky anywhere else.

  • slurmctld stayed Pending. The Paris cluster has no default StorageClass, and the slurm chart's controller.persistence.storageClassName defaults to null, meaning "use the default". The claim never bound. The values now name local-path. A StatefulSet's claim template can't change in place, so the old StatefulSet and its Pending claim had to be deleted for the operator to recreate them. Delete the StatefulSet first, then the claim. In the other order, the old StatefulSet recreates the claim without a class before it goes away, which is what happened here.
  • ArgoCD said Healthy throughout. Slinky's Controller has no status and the NodeSet's is empty, so ArgoCD calls them healthy as soon as they're applied, and the slurmctld pod belongs to the operator, not to the Application. Healthy on slinky means the objects exist. Whether Slurm works is what make slurm-test answers.

  • The pod-cordon drain undid itself. In the first run, the first three checks passed and the fourth didn't:

    $ make slurm-test
...
## 4. Kubernetes to Slurm: nodeset.slinky.slurm.net/pod-cordon=true on slurm-worker-cpu-1   [11:57:19Z]
pod/slurm-worker-cpu-1 annotated
timeout after 120s: cpu-1 drained by the operator
FAIL: cpu-1 not drained
...
1 check(s) failed, see above

    Full capture

    Under the NodeSet's default RollingUpdate strategy, Slinky 1.2.3 drains the Slurm node for an annotated pod, then in the same reconcile removes the annotation from every pod it keeps and undrains the node. The operator logged "Uncordon Pod slurm-worker-cpu-1" one second after the annotation. Slinky's upstream pull request 271 (open) describes the same bug. The NodeSet now uses OnDelete, under which the cordon holds. The cost: a new slurmd image reaches a node only when its pod is deleted, so an upgrade is a drain and a delete per node. - The operator kept restarting. It and its webhook exited with "leader election lost" four times in their first 22 minutes, each time a lease renewal took longer than 5 seconds. The cause wasn't Slinky: Grafana on the Paris control plane was page-faulting its own binary under a 384 Mi memory limit, and the reads starved etcd on the same disk. The limit is now higher. Leader election is also off for both. That's a PoC choice: with one replica there's nothing to elect against. A production install running two replicas keeps it on.

docs.title: Slurm with GPUs at the Finland site: designed, not run
docs.text:
Not built, not run

Nothing in this section was built or run. Running it untested on rented H200 time wasn't worth it, so I wrote down the design instead, from the source at the pinned versions: Slinky slurm-operator and slurm chart 1.2.3, Slurm 26.05.5 (the version inside the pinned slurmd image), GPU Operator v26.7.2, KAI v0.18.6.

docs.title: The NodeSet and GRES for 2x H200
docs.text:
The Finland site would get its own slinky Application, like its own KAI: the operator, slurmctld, the login pod and slurmrestd on the Finland CPU node, with slurmctld's state on that site's local-path, and the keys made by the same bootstrap Job. The new piece is one GPU NodeSet, h200. These values render with slurm chart 1.2.3 into what I'd expect (checked with helm template only):

nodesets:
  h200:
    enabled: true
    replicas: 1                      # one slurmd pod per GPU node
    slurmd:
      env:
        - name: NVIDIA_DRIVER_CAPABILITIES
          value: compute,utility
      resources:
        limits:
          nvidia.com/gpu: 2          # every GPU on the node
    extraConfMap:
      Gres: ["gpu:2"]                # becomes slurmd -Z --conf "Gres=gpu:2"
    updateStrategy:
      type: OnDelete                 # as in Paris, so a pod-cordon drain holds
    podSpec:
      nodeSelector:
        eu1.io/pool: gpu-slurm
      tolerations:
        - key: eu1.io/slurm
          operator: Exists
          effect: NoSchedule
controller:
  extraConfMap:
    GresTypes: [gpu]                 # into slurm.conf
configFiles:
  gres.conf: |
    AutoDetect=nvidia
  cgroup.conf: |
    CgroupPlugin=cgroup/v2
    IgnoreSystemd=yes
    ConstrainDevices=yes             # a job sees only the GPUs Slurm gave it

Three facts from the source decide this shape:

  • The GPUs reach slurmd through the device plugin. The slurmd pod asks for nvidia.com/gpu: 2, and the NVIDIA container runtime injects the driver's libraries and device files. The slurm chart assumes exactly that: its own DCGM integration switches on for any NodeSet with an nvidia.com/gpu limit (templates/vendor/nvidia/dcgm/_helpers.tpl). Inside the pod, Slurm hands GPUs to jobs and ConstrainDevices fences each job to its own.
  • Slinky's slurmd is a dynamic node. The operator starts it as slurmd -Z with the NodeSet's extraConf as --conf (internal/builder/workerbuilder/worker_app.go). So the node's Gres= goes on the NodeSet, not on a NodeName= line, and gres.conf reaches slurmd configless from slurmctld.
  • The pinned slurmd image can see whole GPUs, not MIG. Its layers carry gpu_nvidia.so, gpu_generic.so and gpu_nrt.so under /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/slurm/, but no gpu_nvml.so. Slurm's Debian packaging at 26.05.5 has no NVML build dependency. AutoDetect=nvidia needs no library, "but doesn't detect MIGs or NVlinks" (gres.conf(5) at 26.05.5), and that's enough for two whole H200s.

MIG under Slurm needs AutoDetect=nvml ("To configure MIGs in Slurm, specify AutoDetect=nvml", doc/html/gres.shtml at 26.05.5), so a slurmd image rebuilt with NVML. With h200-split applied, the NodeSet would then ask for nvidia.com/mig-3g.71gb: 2 and nvidia.com/gpu: 1 and declare something like Gres=gpu:h200:1,gpu:3g.71gb:2. Slurm wants each type to be a substring of the "MIG Profile" string slurmd logs at debug2 (its own example is nvidia_a100_3g.20gb), so the exact names get read on the node, not guessed. Slurm doesn't partition MIG itself; the GPU Operator's MIG manager would, from the same node label as in use case 4. And Slurm keeps no gpumem or gpuutil accounting for MIG devices, because NVML has none. Unlike KAI, Slurm would use the whole GPU next to the slices, since slurmd's pod isn't scheduled by KAI.

docs.title: A GPU check in the prolog
docs.text:
The prolog in Paris, 00-node-health.sh, checks /tmp, free memory and the simulated fault marker. On a GPU node, a second script would run after it:

# 10-gpu-health.sh: DCGM's quickest diagnostic on this job's GPUs, before the job starts.
[ -n "${SLURM_JOB_GPUS:-}" ] || exit 0          # not a GPU job
dcgmi diag -r 1 --host nvidia-dcgm.gpu-operator.svc:5555 -i "$DCGM_IDS" \
  || { echo "GPU health: dcgmi diag -r 1 failed" >&2; exit 1; }

A failure drains the node and holds the job, as the simulated fault did in Paris. The pieces come from the Finland site's existing stack: the base values run the GPU Operator's standalone DCGM (dcgm.enabled: true), and at v26.7.2 the operator puts it behind Service nvidia-dcgm, port 5555, with internalTrafficPolicy: Local (assets/state-dcgm/0500_service.yaml). So a prolog on a node always talks to that node's own hostengine. Two things stay open. dcgmi isn't in the slurmd image, so it comes with the NVML rebuild. And $DCGM_IDS has to map Slurm's GPU indices to DCGM's by UUID, because nothing guarantees the two number the GPUs the same way.

Level 1 is the cheapest check DCGM has, which suits a run before every job. The deeper dcgmi diag -r 2 that NVCRE runs in the certification gate stays where it is, before a node opens to tenants. Slurm's HealthCheckProgram could run something in between on an interval, while the node idles. Node-level faults need no new code at all: NVSentinel already cordons a node on a GPU fault (use case 3), and a cordoned Kubernetes node makes Slinky drain its Slurm node, with the reason "Node (…) was cordoned" (syncCordon in internal/controller/nodeset/nodeset_sync.go). That path skips pod uncordoning, so it holds under any update strategy.

docs.title: How KAI and Slurm split the Finland GPUs
docs.text:
By whole node, never by GPU:

  • A node belongs to one of them. Slurm's GPU nodes carry eu1.io/pool: gpu-slurm and the taint eu1.io/slurm=true:NoSchedule. KAI's tenants select eu1.io/pool: gpu and tolerate neither. That's the pattern Slinky's own workload-isolation guide uses, a taint the NodeSet tolerates (docs/usage/workload-isolation.md).
  • Never the same GPU. slurmd's pod takes every GPU on its node through the device plugin. Even a pod that slipped past the label and the taint would find no GPU left to allocate. The device plugin, not a convention, is what keeps the two schedulers apart.
  • The certification gate applies to both. A new H200 joins with eu1.io/staging=pending:NoSchedule, and the slurmd pod doesn't tolerate it, exactly like KAI's pods. Slurm only ever sees a node after NVCRE has certified it and the gate has opened it.
  • Moving a node between them is maintenance: cordon it, which makes Slinky drain its Slurm node, wait for the jobs to finish, delete the slurmd pod, then change the label and taint. The H200 run on 22 October gave one more reason to split per node: KAI v0.18.6 won't place a whole-GPU pod on a node with MIG on (ADR 0008), so the Finland node pools already have to be whole-GPU or MIG, node by node.

KAI could also schedule the slurmd pods themselves, through an hpc queue whose quota is the Slurm nodes' GPUs, so one fair-share view covers both. I'd leave that out at first. KAI could then reclaim a slurmd pod like any over-quota workload, and with it every Slurm job on that node.

docs.title: The 580 driver and the CUDA in slurmd
docs.text:
The Finland image ships driver 580.178.04. The R580 branch is CUDA 13.0's own; CUDA 13.1 to 13.4 belong to R590 through R615. They run on 580 in two ways. One is minor-version compatibility ("13.x: >= 580" in NVIDIA's CUDA Toolkit release notes, read 22 October), which has limits: anything that needs a newer driver fails, and PTX built by a newer toolkit can't be compiled by the older driver. The other is the forward-compatibility libraries that NGC images carry. The H200 run saw both, in the same CUDA 13.1 image (NVCRE's NCCL log). The all-reduce job, under MPI, reported cudaDriverVersion 13010, so it had loaded the image's forward-compatibility libcuda. The single-process loopback job reported 13000: minor-version compatibility on the host's driver. So jobs at the Finland site get CUDA 13.0 natively, and anything newer only through one of those two routes, each with its own catch.

The pinned slurmd image holds no CUDA at all. Its environment sets none, its layers carry no libcuda, and the driver's libraries arrive from the container runtime. So a job's CUDA comes from one of two places:

  • The slurmd image itself, rebuilt with the tenant's stack, as Slinky's PyTorch tutorial does (docs/usage/tutorial-pytorch.md). That puts every tenant on one image, which Nordhaven would have to keep within CUDA 13.0.
  • The job's own container, through pyxis and enroot (docs/usage/pyxis.md, with Slinky's slurmd-pyxis image). Tenants bring their image, and Nordhaven keeps one slurmd. Part 1's trainer image, CUDA 12.8, ran natively on this driver in the H200 run. The cost is that Slinky's pyxis guide runs the login container privileged so enroot works there.

For a group with its own software stack, I'd pick pyxis: it keeps the CUDA choice with the tenant, and the platform's job is only to publish the ceiling.

docs.title: Why it wasn't run
docs.text:
• Cost. Every minute at the Finland site is a rented H200. Slurm with GPUs needs its own operator and controller there, then the node taken away from KAI, which on 22 October would have meant fewer minutes for the gang and MIG.
  • No check without a GPU reaches the parts that matter. I can render the charts, dry-run the objects on a cluster and parse the Slurm config without a GPU. Whether AutoDetect=nvidia finds both GPUs inside the pod, whether ConstrainDevices fences them per job, and whether a prolog can reach DCGM only show on a GPU node.

docs.title: What one VM can't show
docs.text:
• Two machines. Both Slurm nodes run on one VM (oversubscribeNode, which Slinky marks as not for production).
  • GPUs in Slurm. The Paris Slurm is CPU-only, and Slurm on the Finland H200s isn't built. The design is above.
  • Shared storage. With no ReadWriteMany volume, a job's output stays on the node that ran it.
  • Accounting and fair share over time. No slurmdbd.
  • Performance next to a bare-metal Slurm. Not measured.

docs.title: One view of GPU metrics across two sites, with Thanos
docs.text:
The use case

Nordhaven has a permanent site in Paris, and a site in Finland that only exists while its H200s are rented. Nordhaven wants one place to query every GPU of both sites, and the Finland metrics have to stay queryable after the Finland site is deleted. Here Finland writes to Thanos Receive in Paris, Paris keeps its own Prometheus with a sidecar, and one Thanos Query reads both and the bucket. The design and its alternatives (Mimir, VictoriaMetrics) are in ADR 0009.

What ran

The Paris side ran on 21 October: Receive, the sidecar, deduplication, uploads, and downsampling on simulated blocks. A CPU-only test of the Finland site on the same day carried its metrics to Paris over the internet. On 22 October the Finland site ran with two H200s for about half an hour. Their DCGM series reached Paris, first on whole GPUs and then with one H200 split by MIG. They were still queryable in Paris after the Finland site was deleted.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  subgraph fin["Finland (exists only while its GPUs are rented)"]
    fprom["Prometheus<br/>site=fin"]
  end
  subgraph par["Paris (permanent)"]
    pprom["Prometheus + Thanos sidecar<br/>site=par, control plane"]
    recv["Thanos Receive<br/>CPU worker, NodePort 30291"]
    q["Thanos Query"]
    sg["Store gateway"]
    comp["Compactor<br/>downsampling"]
    bucket[("Garage bucket thanos")]
    graf["Grafana<br/>EU1 GPUs across sites"]
  end
  fprom -- "remote write, mutual TLS<br/>client CN = tenant" --> recv
  pprom -- "2 h blocks" --> bucket
  recv -- "2 h blocks" --> bucket
  comp <--> bucket
  sg --> bucket
  q --> pprom
  q --> recv
  q --> sg
  graf --> q
  • Finland pushes, Paris never reaches in. The Finland firewall opens nothing to Paris, and Paris can't query a site that's been deleted. Port 30291 on the Paris CPU worker is open only to the Finland node addresses. Tested from my laptop, it doesn't answer.
  • The certificate names the tenant. Receive takes the tenant from the client certificate's common name, so the Finland site can only write as fin. The CA is generated in the cluster by a Job and never goes into Git.
  • Paris doesn't depend on the CPU worker. The Paris Prometheus stays on the control plane and uploads through a sidecar. It keeps working, alerting included, while the worker that runs Receive, Query and the compactor is powered off.

docs.title: The Paris hub, 21 October

Before renting H200s, I tested the Finland write path with a Finland control plane on a CPU instance (CPU.8V.32G, FIN-01). The first attempt never got a machine: at 12:16 UTC the provider put the instance in status "error". The retry ran from 15:33 to 15:40 UTC (while it ran, after deletion):

That covered what only a real Finland site could test: port 30291 open to its actual address, the certificate reaching it, and remote write across the internet.

It also taught me something about querying a deleted site. An instant query only sees a series for 5 minutes after its last sample. My first query asked for "now", 16 minutes after the site was gone, and found nothing, although Receive held all of it. Queries about a deleted site have to look back, as MODE=after now does (last_over_time(...[3h])), and a dashboard showing it needs a time range that covers the run.

docs.title: Series per GPU, and what they mean for capacity
docs.text:
From the L4 run in Paris on 21 October (capture, follow-up) and the H200 run in Finland:

GPU DCGM series L4, idle 40 L4, under the training job 41 (DCGM_EXP_CLOCK_EVENTS_TOTAL{clock_event="power_cap"} appeared) H200, whole 40, then 41 under load H200 split into two MIG instances 51 (11 for the device, 20 per instance)

Two things make the count move, both visible in the labels:

  • One series per clock-event reason. gpu_idle was there from the start. power_cap appeared when the training job hit the L4's power limit.
  • Pod labels on a busy GPU. dcgm-exporter adds exported_pod, exported_namespace and exported_container to the series of a GPU a pod is using. Every new job puts its own pod name on new series, so the count churns with the workload, not only with the number of GPUs.

So the per-GPU figure for capacity planning is the maximum over a busy period, not an idle reading. The recording rule is evaluated every minute and kept with the rest of the data, so max_over_time(gpu:dcgm_series:count[...]) gives it.

At 40 to 51 series per GPU, 1,000 GPUs make 40,000 to 51,000 DCGM series and 10,000 GPUs make 400,000 to 510,000, before pod-label churn. That is arithmetic from three GPUs, not a load test. For scale, the DCGM series were 91 of the 66,491 series in the Finland Prometheus: almost all of the rest came from the control plane's API server and kubelets.

docs.title: What's simulated
docs.text:
Both are listed in what is simulated and labelled on every series:

  • site="fin-sim": a second Prometheus in Paris posing as the Finland site, writing through the same mutual TLS path.
  • site="sim-backfill": the synthetic blocks for the downsampling check.

The H200 series, the L4 series and the Finland write path are real.

docs.title: What two sites and three GPUs can't show
docs.text:
• A Receive hashring or replication. There is one Receive and one site writing to it, so the write path has a single point of failure. The Finland Prometheus keeps its WAL and retries through a short outage.
  • Cardinality at scale. The figures above for 1,000 and 10,000 GPUs are extrapolated, not load-tested.
  • Downsampling of real data, until the Paris uploads span two days.
  • The Finland site's last block in the bucket. The Finland data sits in Receive's head. It reaches the bucket when Receive cuts a block or stops, as the 12 second fin-sim block above shows. I haven't listed the bucket since the H200 run.

docs.title: VM tenants next to the GPU pods, with KubeVirt
docs.text:
The use case

Some of Nordhaven's tenants can't move to containers yet. They ship a whole operating system image, or a licensed appliance, or software that expects to own a kernel. Nordhaven wants to sell them capacity from the same fleet, run by the same people and tools. Here a VM runs on the Paris CPU worker as a Kubernetes object, under a tenant quota, next to the GPU workloads, and the guest itself says it runs on KVM. The choice of KubeVirt over a separate IaaS is in ADR 0010.

What ran

On 21 October in Paris: KubeVirt v1.9.1 deployed by ArgoCD, and a VM, web-01, booted on KVM under the tenant-vm quota. It kept running through the day, including while a training job used the Paris L4 on another node. Nothing in this use case is simulated.

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  argo["ArgoCD Application kubevirt<br/>wave 10"] --> op["virt-operator<br/>1 replica, CPU worker"]
  op --> cr["KubeVirt resource<br/>useEmulation: false"]
  cr --> api["virt-api, virt-controller,<br/>export proxy, virt-template"]
  cr --> handler["virt-handler<br/>DaemonSet, CPU worker only"]
  wait["Sync hook Job<br/>waits for Available"] --> tenant["tenant-vm: quota,<br/>VM web-01, Service"]
  handler --> launcher["virt-launcher pod<br/>QEMU/KVM, the guest"]
  tenant --> launcher

Everything sits on eu1-par-cpu-01, a Scaleway POP2-8C-32G that exposes /dev/kvm with AMD SVM (node facts). Nothing runs on the 4 vCPU control plane.

docs.title: What I had to change from the release manifest
docs.text:
Each of these comes from reading KubeVirt's source at v1.9.1:

  • virt-operator insists on a control-plane node. Its release Deployment requires one, with no override (components/deployments.go). A kustomize patch moves it to the CPU worker as one replica. The KubeVirt resource's nodePlacement places the rest.
  • ArgoCD can't tell when KubeVirt is ready. ArgoCD v3.5.3 has health checks for VirtualMachine but not for the KubeVirt resource, so it would apply the tenant's VM before the operator had created the VM's CRD. A Sync hook Job waits for Available first.
  • A digest on the operator doesn't pin what it deploys. The operator builds each component's image from its version as a tag, unless that component's *_IMAGE variable is set. So thirteen are set by digest (pin-images.yaml). The first deployment showed two I had missed: the virt-template components. They deploy by default, because their gate is Beta and KubeVirt turns Beta gates on, and they follow their own release, v0.2.3. They ran from tags until I pinned them too (before, after).

docs.text:
The quota counts what the cluster really reserves for the VM, which is more than the guest gets:

Container in the virt-launcher pod CPU request Memory request compute (QEMU, libvirt and the guest) 1 2316 Mi, for a 2 GiB guest guest-console-log (sidecar init container) 5m 35 M Counted by the tenant-vm quota 1005m 2349 Mi

docs.text:

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: Two sites, two providers, one repository. Paris stays up between GPU runs: a small control plane and a CPU worker that I power off when nothing needs it, plus an L4 node created for a GPU run and destroyed after. The whole Finland site, control plane included, exists only while I rent its H200 node. Everything that runs in either cluster comes from ArgoCD reading main; a person runs terraform through make, and git push.

The driver is the one exception, and it's deliberate: Paris runs 595.91.07, installed by the GPU Operator as in Part 1, and Finland runs 580.178.04 from Verda's image (ADR 0002).
