  • medik8s: node-healthcheck-operator README and docs/configuration.md at v0.12.0 (default unhealthy conditions: Ready False or Unknown for 300 s), self-node-remediation README.

docs.title: ADR 0006: Batch scheduling for many tenants, KAI Scheduler over Kueue and Volcano
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: batch scheduling for GPU tenants, both sites (use case 4). Decided after the H200 run, 22 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Nordhaven sells scarce GPUs to several tenants at once. Each tenant wants a guaranteed share, the right to borrow what others leave idle, and its distributed jobs started whole or not at all, since half a training job holds GPUs and does nothing. In Part 1, two tenants shared one L4 through time slicing with a plain ResourceQuota: the quota capped each tenant, but nothing lent idle GPUs, took them back, or placed a job as a unit.

The constraint that decides most of this is the GPU stack Nordhaven already runs: the NVIDIA GPU Operator, whose device plugin advertises nvidia.com/gpu and, at the Finland site, MIG slices. Whatever schedules tenants has to work with that device plugin rather than replace it.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. KAI Scheduler v0.18.6 A second scheduler (from Run:ai, now a CNCF Sandbox project) for pods that set schedulerName: kai-scheduler, with hierarchical queues and its own pod grouper Quota, over-quota borrowing by weight, and reclaim of borrowed GPUs are queue fields (scheduling.run.ai/v2 Queue). The pod grouper turns a Job, JobSet or PyTorchJob into a gang without a hand-written PodGroup (kai.scheduler/batch-min-member). It reads MIG resources by name (pkg/scheduler/api/common_info/resources/mig.go) and can share a GPU in fractions. NVIDIA's AICR v1.1.0 ships it in its base recipe Two schedulers in one cluster. Its webhooks fail closed, though only for KAI's own pods and Queues (matchConditions in pkg/operator/operands/admission/resources.go). The operator builds its images from a tag, so they can't be pinned by digest. Tags v0.20.0 and v0.20.1 were published, then retracted B. Kueue v0.20.2 A quota and admission layer from Kubernetes SIG Scheduling in front of the default kube-scheduler: ClusterQueues, cohorts, borrowing, fair sharing, preemption kube-scheduler stays the only scheduler. It has the widest set of integrations, MultiKueue for several clusters, and topology-aware scheduling It admits quota, then kube-scheduler places pods one by one. All-or-nothing is timeout-based: pods that bound wait until waitForPodsReady gives up and requeues the job, holding their GPUs meanwhile. It can't share a GPU; a fraction has to come from somewhere else C. Volcano v1.16.0 A batch scheduler built on kube-batch, CNCF incubating, with its own Job, PodGroup and Queue Gangs, queues, reclaim and network-topology placement (HyperNode) all in one scheduler. Spark, Kubeflow and LeaderWorkerSet integrate with it Also a second scheduler. Its GPU sharing goes through its own vGPU device plugin (docs/user-guide/how_to_use_volcano_vgpu.md), which would sit beside or replace the GPU Operator's. NVIDIA's reference stack doesn't carry it

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
KAI Scheduler, pinned at v0.18.6.

Two reasons decided it. KAI does the three things Nordhaven needs in one place: queue shares with borrowing and reclaim, gangs placed as a unit by the scheduler itself (not admitted, then placed pod by pod), and MIG and fractions counted against queues. All of that runs on top of the GPU Operator's device plugin, untouched. And it is what AICR, NVIDIA's own known-good stack, installs, so Nordhaven's choice matches what an NVIDIA architect expects to find.

On the version: v0.18 is KAI's active long-term-support line, supported from September 2026 to September 2027, and upstream validates v0.16 to v0.18 on Kubernetes v1.36.1. Both facts come from SUPPORT.md on main, read 21 October; the copy inside the v0.18.6 tag was written before the v0.18 line existed and doesn't list it. AICR v1.1.0 resolves v0.16.9, the previous LTS line, now in maintenance. v0.16.12 already exists on that line, so AICR is three patches behind. AICR is a reference only in this project (ADR 0003), and KAI isn't part of the Finland site's base, so Nordhaven runs the newer line and records the difference.

What would change the answer:

  • A partner that already runs Kueue for CPU batch, or needs MultiKueue across clusters, should keep Kueue for admission and accept timeout-based gangs, or evaluate it in front of KAI. That combination isn't tested here.
  • A partner whose tenants are mostly Spark or big data jobs: Volcano's integrations there are older and deeper.
  • Tenants that never share a GPU and never run multi-pod jobs: kube-scheduler and a ResourceQuota, as in Part 1, are enough. A second scheduler would only add something to operate.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Tenants get shares, borrowing and reclaim from queue fields instead of a ticket to an operator. A workload joins KAI with one label and one schedulerName. Pods that don't ask for KAI are untouched.
  • Nordhaven now operates a second scheduler: the operator, scheduler, binder, admission, pod grouper and queue controller, about 1.5 vCPU requested on the Paris CPU worker. KAI's own pods and Queue writes stop when the worker is off; other workloads' pods don't.
  • ArgoCD needs a health check for KAI's Config and SchedulingShard. argocd-cm carries one, taken from KAI's GitOps doc at v0.18.6.
  • Operand images run by tag (v0.18.6), not by digest. That's an exception to rule 7, kept because the operator has no digest field.
  • What this PoC can't show:
  • the Paris queues run on simulated GPUs: two KWOK nodes, where pods bind but no container runs (docs/simulated.md)
  • a gang across nodes: the Finland site has one node with two GPUs, so its gang is two pods on one machine
  • fairness over time: KAI's time-aware fairness needs its Prometheus integration, which is off
  • behaviour at hundreds of nodes and thousands of queued pods

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Checks without a GPU: renders, digests, a dry run at the Paris site; KAI's chart generates no secret at render time, and every KAI pod lands on the site's pool.
  • KAI's SUPPORT.md on main, read 21 October (support dates and the Kubernetes matrix for v0.16 to v0.18; the copy at v0.18.6 stops at v0.17).
  • Source at v0.18.6: docs/queues/README.md, docs/batch/README.md, docs/gitops/README.md, pkg/scheduler/api/common_info/resources/mig.go, pkg/operator/operands/admission/resources.go. AICR v1.1.0: docs/user/component-version-matrix.md, recipes/overlays/base.yaml. Kueue's README at v0.20.2 ("All-or-nothing with ready Pods"). Volcano's README and docs/user-guide/how_to_use_volcano_vgpu.md at v1.16.0.
  • Paris, simulated GPUs, 21 October (capture): team-a borrowed 4 GPUs over its quota; team-b's gang of 4 made KAI evict exactly those 4 and bind all 4 gang pods 2 seconds later; a gang of 6 with 4 GPUs free bound nothing, with KAI's reason on the PodGroup.
  • Paris, CPU worker, 21 October (capture): the two-pod gang with real containers, bound in the same second, all-reduce over gloo completed.
  • Finland, two H200s, 22 October (capture, NCCL logs): the two-pod gang bound in the same second, with one GPU borrowed from idle team-b, and a gang of 3 on 2 GPUs bound nothing. Between the two pods NCCL ran over NET/Socket on the pod network at 2.24 GB/s, against 351 GB/s over NVLink inside one pod (NVCRE's report, use case 2). The use case 4 page shows the outputs.

docs.title: ADR 0007: HPC tenants on the same platform, Slurm through Slinky
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: Slurm for HPC tenants, on the Paris CPU pool (use case 5); GPUs in Slurm designed, not built.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
One of Nordhaven's first customers is a research group that has used Slurm for years. Its scripts call sbatch, srun and squeue, and its people won't rewrite them as Kubernetes Jobs to rent GPUs. Nordhaven doesn't want a second fleet for them either: the same nodes, the same GPU Operator, the same monitoring and the same health story as its Kubernetes tenants.

What narrows the choice is what Nordhaven already runs. The Paris site is upstream Kubernetes 1.36 with flannel, local-path volumes (ReadWriteOnce only), cert-manager and the GPU Operator. The Finland site's driver is 580, the branch Verda's image ships, kept as it is (ADR 0002).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. Slinky 1.2.3 SchedMD's slurm-operator: Slurm's controller, login nodes and slurmd run as pods described by Controller, LoginSet and NodeSet objects Stock Slurm 26.05 from the people who make Slurm. It runs on what the Paris site already has: flannel, local-path, cert-manager for its webhook. Kubernetes and Slurm see each other: cordoning a node drains its Slurm node, and Slurm states show up as pod conditions (docs/concepts/nodeset-controller.md). AICR v1.1.0 lists Slurm through Slinky as a platform, and NVSentinel has a slinky-drainer slurmd runs in a pod, so jobs share the pod's limits and the node with Kubernetes workloads. Accounting needs a MariaDB. Its chart makes its auth keys with lookup and randAscii, which ArgoCD can't render stably (a finding; worked around with a bootstrap Job) B. Soperator 4.1.14 (Nebius) An operator that builds a Slurm cluster from one SlurmCluster object, with a shared root filesystem (the "jail") and health checks Complete for GPU training: the training stack and health checks come with it, and the shared root keeps nodes identical The jail needs a shared filesystem ("at least one shared filesystem is necessary", README at 4.1.14), and the Paris site has only ReadWriteOnce local-path. At 4.1.14 it supports Slurm 25.11.3 and CUDA 12.9, a Slurm release behind Slinky's 26.05, and one partition per cluster. The tag disagrees with itself on CPU nodes: the README allows a CPU-only cluster, docs/limitations.md says GPUs are required. Its main branch already moves to CUDA newer than 13.0, which the Finland site's 580 driver runs only through minor-version compatibility or an image's forward-compatibility libraries, each with its limits C. A separate Slurm cluster Slurm installed on its own VMs or bare metal, outside Kubernetes What the research group already knows, with no container layer between Slurm and the hardware A second fleet, provisioned, monitored and repaired another way. GPUs given to it are lost to Kubernetes tenants until someone moves them by hand D. No Slurm Ask the group to submit Kubernetes Jobs through KAI's queues One scheduler path, nothing new to run It asks the customer to change, which is the thing Nordhaven is trying to avoid

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Slinky.

Two things decided it. It's stock Slurm 26.05 from SchedMD, running on exactly the pieces the Paris site already has. Soperator 4.1.14 needs a shared filesystem Paris doesn't have, and its own documents disagree on whether the Paris CPU-only worker can host it. Its next release also raises the CUDA floor above what the Finland 580 driver runs natively. And Slinky's two-way link between Kubernetes and Slurm is what lets Nordhaven keep one operations story: cordon a node for maintenance and Slurm drains it; a Slurm drain shows up on the pod where the platform's tools already look.

What would change the answer:

  • A partner with fast shared storage and a current driver everywhere, running large GPU training: Soperator's jail and active checks save real work at that scale, and its rising CUDA floor stops mattering.
  • An HPC group that needs bare-metal performance and never shares nodes: a separate Slurm cluster, accepting the second fleet.
  • A group willing to move to Kubernetes Jobs: KAI alone (ADR 0006).

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The research group keeps sbatch and srun, logging into a login pod. Nordhaven runs one more operator, a controller with a 2 GB volume, a REST API and the slurmd pods, all on the Paris CPU worker.
  • Slurm's auth keys are created once in the cluster by a bootstrap Job, never in Git, never rotated by a sync.
  • A prolog health check runs before every job: a node that fails it is drained and the job held, the Slurm side of the readiness gate in use case 2.
  • No accounting: sacct and fair share over time need slurmdbd and a MariaDB, which this PoC doesn't run.
  • GPUs in Slurm would take whole nodes out of KAI's pool, never single GPUs: slurmd's pod holds every GPU on its node through the device plugin, and both schedulers sit behind the same certification gate. The design, including GRES for the H200s and their MIG slices, a DCGM check in the prolog and the CUDA ceiling of the Finland 580 driver, is on the use case 5 page; it isn't built or run. The pinned slurmd image can't see MIG at all (no gpu_nvml plugin).
  • The slurmd NodeSet uses the OnDelete update strategy. Under the default, RollingUpdate, Slinky 1.2.3 releases a drain requested through the pod-cordon annotation within the same reconcile (Slinky's upstream pull request 271, and a finding). The cost: a new slurmd image reaches a node only when its pod is deleted, so upgrades are a deliberate drain-and-delete per node.
  • ArgoCD's Healthy says little about this app. Slinky's Controller has no status and the NodeSet's is empty, so ArgoCD reports them healthy as soon as they're applied, and the pods belong to the operator, not the Application. On 21 October slinky read Healthy while slurmctld sat Pending on an unbound volume. Whether Slurm works is what make slurm-test answers.
  • What this PoC can't show:
  • two Slurm nodes on one VM (oversubscribeNode, which Slinky marks as not for production), standing in for two machines
  • GPUs in Slurm: the Paris Slurm is CPU-only, and Slurm on the Finland H200s isn't built
  • shared storage: with no ReadWriteMany volume, a job's output stays on the node that ran it
  • performance next to a bare-metal Slurm

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Checks without a GPU: renders, digests, CR schemas, a dry run at the Paris site. Every Slinky pod lands on the CPU pool, the chart renders no generated Secret, and the webhook CA comes from cert-manager.
  • Source at the pinned versions: Slinky slurm-operator 1.2.3 README.md (compatibility matrix) and docs/concepts/nodeset-controller.md; api/v1beta1/well_known.go (the pod-cordon annotation); slurm chart 1.2.3 templates/secrets/slurmkey.yaml. Soperator at 4.1.14 (tagged 20 October): README.md ("Shared root filesystem", "Limitations", the first installation step) and docs/limitations.md ("GPUs are required", "Single-partition clusters"). Soperator's README on main, read 21 October, for the next requirements (CUDA newer than 13.0, Slurm 26.05.4-nebius-1, Kubernetes 1.35 or newer); not released at the time of writing. AICR v1.1.0 README and docs/user/component-catalog.md (slinky-drainer).
  • make slurm-test at the Paris site, 21 October. First run: srun -N2, sbatch and the prolog drain passed; the pod-cordon drain didn't hold, which led to the OnDelete change above. Second run, after it: all four checks pass, and the annotation drains the Slurm node within 6 seconds, with the operator's reason in sinfo -R and SlurmNodeStateDrain=True on the pod. Cordoning a whole Kubernetes node drives the same code path, but the test doesn't do it, because the Paris CPU worker is shared with other workloads.
  • The use case 5 page walks through both runs and the four problems the first sync turned up.
  • Slinky 1.2.3 source behind the first failure: internal/controller/nodeset/nodeset_sync.go (syncCordon, then syncPodUncordon from doPodProcessing), and Slinky's upstream pull request 271.

docs.title: ADR 0008: GPU sharing per tenant class, MIG for small tenants and whole GPUs for training
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: GPU sharing per tenant class, on the Finland H200s and the Paris L4 (use case 4). Decided after the H200 run, 22 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Not every Nordhaven tenant needs a whole GPU. A notebook, a small fine-tune or a low-traffic inference endpoint uses a fraction of an H200's 141 GB and 132 SMs. Selling a whole GPU to each of them wastes capacity, while packing them onto one GPU means one tenant's crash, memory leak or noisy kernel can reach the others.

Part 1 packed two tenants onto one L4 with time slicing (ts-4, four replicas). The capture shows three pods from two tenants all reporting the same GPU UUID, with each tenant's ResourceQuota refusing a third pod. Time slicing has no isolation: tenants share the GPU's memory and its fault domain. Part 1 stated that an XID from one tenant drains everyone on the node, and its remediation controller drains the node on an XID. The XID 79 injection on that L4 is captured (19:48:35Z, with the tenants running since 19:40:55Z). The tenant pods themselves being evicted is not; it follows from the drain, but no artifact shows it.

The L4 has no MIG. The Finland H200s do.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. Whole GPUs One tenant per GPU, nvidia.com/gpu: 1 Full isolation, nothing to configure, what training jobs want anyway Wastes most of an H200 on a small tenant; on a 2-GPU node, two small tenants exhaust it B. Time slicing The device plugin advertises N replicas of each GPU; the GPU switches between processes Works on any GPU, the L4 included. One ConfigMap. Proven in Part 1 No memory limit and one fault domain: one tenant can take all the memory, and a fault drains everyone. Replicas are counted, not sized, so a "quarter GPU" guarantees nothing C. MPS The device plugin runs an MPS daemon; clients share the GPU concurrently with per-client memory and thread limits Real concurrency and a memory cap per client. Works without MIG All clients sit behind one MPS server and share its fault domain, so a fatal error in one client affects the others. Better for one tenant's many processes than for several paying tenants D. MIG The GPU splits in hardware into instances, each with its own SMs, memory slice and L2 Each tenant gets dedicated memory and compute, with fault containment per instance. The device plugin advertises each profile as its own resource (nvidia.com/mig-3g.71gb), and KAI counts it against the tenant's queue Only on MIG-capable GPUs, so not on the Paris L4. The layout is fixed per node: changing it means stopping every GPU client on that GPU, which mig-manager does by pausing the operands. A GPU-wide fault (the GPU falling off the bus, XID 79) still takes every instance E. KAI fractions KAI places pods asking for gpu-fraction on a shared GPU and reserves the rest Fine-grained, no hardware support needed NonMemoryEnforced, KAI's default mode: a placement promise, not isolation. The same fault domain as time slicing

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Sharing depends on the tenant class and the hardware, not one setting for the whole fleet:

  • Training tenants get whole GPUs, as a gang through KAI (ADR 0006), on nodes with MIG off. At the Finland site, that's both GPUs while the node runs without MIG.
  • Small tenants on MIG-capable GPUs get MIG instances. At the Finland site, the h200-split layout makes GPU0 into two 3g.71gb instances, one per tenant, each with about 70 GiB of its own. MIG is the only option here where a tenant's memory and faults stay inside what it pays for, and isolation between paying tenants is the property Nordhaven sells.
  • The split between the two is per node, not per GPU. I first designed one node with both: MIG slices on GPU0 for small tenants, GPU1 whole for a training job. The H200 run on 22 October showed KAI v0.18.6 won't do that. On a MIG-enabled node with nvidia.com/mig.strategy=mixed, it refuses every task that isn't a MIG request ("non MIG jobs cant run on a node with MigStrategy='mixed'", pkg/scheduler/api/node_info/node_info.go), although the GPU Operator still advertises the whole GPU. So Nordhaven runs MIG nodes and whole-GPU nodes as separate pools, and a MIG node's layout should slice every GPU it has. In h200-split as written, GPU1 is stranded under KAI.
  • The Paris L4 pool stays time-sliced only for a single tenant's own pods (dev and CI), never between two paying tenants. Without MIG on the L4, the honest offer to a second tenant is a whole L4.

What would change the answer:

  • MIG-capable GPUs in the inference pool: the Paris small tenants would move to MIG too, and time slicing would disappear from the tenant offer.
  • A tenant with many processes and one trust domain (one team's inference fleet): MPS on its own GPUs beats MIG on utilization, because there are no fixed slice sizes.
  • Demand that changes hour by hour: fixed MIG layouts strand capacity. Then layouts per node pool, set at node creation, or dynamic resource allocation once it's ready for MIG in this stack, are worth the work. This PoC doesn't test either.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Two tenants on one H200, each with its own memory, SMs and fault containment, scheduled through the same KAI queues as whole-GPU jobs, but on different nodes from them.
  • Capacity planning works in nodes: deciding how many nodes are MIG nodes, and with which layout, is the operator's lever. On a fleet of 2-GPU nodes that's coarse, and the Finland site's single node can show one mode at a time.
  • MIG is a node property Nordhaven operates: the layout lives in the GPU Operator overlay (gitops/values/scheduling/gpu-operator-fin.yaml), named after what it does (Part 1 rule 6), and a node label selects it. Changing it pauses that node's GPU clients, so layout changes are maintenance, not self-service.
  • WITH_REBOOT stays false: if a mode change fails, the node reports failed instead of rebooting itself while tenants wait for it.
  • What this PoC can't show:
  • fault containment between MIG instances: no fault was injected on the H200s, so the isolation comes from NVIDIA's MIG documentation, not a capture
  • MIG at the Paris site: the L4 doesn't support it
  • more than one layout, or a layout change under load: the H200 run applied h200-split once
  • MPS: not deployed

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Part 1 (nvidia-gpu-fleet-poc): docs/artifacts/session-d-tenancy.txt and session-d-tenancy-verdict.txt (three pods, two tenants, one L4 UUID, the quota refusal), session-d-timeline.txt (xid_injected=2026-09-30T19:48:35.363Z ... xid=79 simulated=true), docs/04-goodput-and-burn-in.md ("Time slicing has no isolation").
  • A check of the MIG config without a GPU: the GPU Operator v26.7.2 render for the Finland site has mig.strategy=mixed, the mig-parted-eu1 ConfigMap and WITH_REBOOT=false (capture).
  • Source: mig-parted v0.15.1, pkg/mig/reconfigure/reconfigure.go (state labels, the reboot fallback) and cmd/nvidia-mig-parted/util/device.go (nvidia-smi -r on a pending mode change); KAI v0.18.6, pkg/scheduler/api/common_info/resources/mig.go; H200 141GB profiles from NVIDIA's MIG user guide.
  • make sched-mig-check, 21 October (capture): the Finland rendered config through mig-parted v0.15.1's own loader on the Paris CPU worker. h200-split and all-disabled are valid, an unknown name is refused.
  • MIG on the H200 node, 22 October (capture): h200-split applied in 33 seconds with no reboot; team-a and team-b each ran on their own 3g.71gb instance of the same H200, and CUDA saw 69.8 GiB in each.
  • The whole-GPU pod beside them, refused (capture): resubmitted alone and within quota, KAI still held it with "1 non MIG jobs cant run on a node with MigStrategy='mixed'". Source: KAI v0.18.6, pkg/scheduler/api/node_info/node_info.go.
  • make sched-mig-check, 22 October (capture): all-disabled, h200-split and the RTX PRO 6000 layout rtxpro-split all valid. The use case 4 page shows the outputs.

docs.title: ADR 0009: Metrics across sites, Thanos Receive for Finland and a sidecar for Paris
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: observability, both sites (use case 6). Decided after the H200 run, 22 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Nordhaven has a permanent site in Paris, and a site in Finland that only exists while its GPUs are rented. make fin-down deletes the Finland site with its disks, so whatever its Prometheus holds goes with it unless it has already left. Nordhaven wants one view of the L4 in Paris and the H200s in Finland, and that view has to keep showing the Finland GPUs after the site is gone.

Two facts narrow the choice before any product comparison: the Finland site opens no port to Paris (its firewall allows SSH and the Kubernetes API from admin ranges only), and Paris can't query a site that no longer exists. Whatever carries the Finland metrics has to push them out of Finland while the site is still running.

Thanos was the starting point. Mimir and VictoriaMetrics answer the same question, so they're in the table too.

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text: Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. Thanos sidecar Prometheus stays where it is; a sidecar uploads its 2 hour blocks to object storage and serves recent data over gRPC to a central Thanos Query Nothing extra in the write path. A WAN outage loses nothing, because the data waits at the site. Each site keeps alerting locally Prometheus only turns its head into a block once the head spans 1.5 times the block range, 3 hours (compactable() in tsdb/head.go at v3.14.0). A site rented for 2 hours is deleted before the first upload. And Query has to dial into Finland for recent data, which means an inbound port on a site that gets deleted B. Thanos Receive Prometheus remote-writes to Receive, which builds the blocks and uploads them The Finland site only needs to reach out. Samples are in Paris within seconds. Receive flushes its head and uploads the last block when it stops (cmd/thanos/receive.go L725-736 and L818-832 at v0.42.4). It can take the tenant from the client certificate, so one credential authenticates and names the site One more component in the write path. At scale it needs a hashring and a replication factor of 3, which triples the ingest work. The sender keeps a remote write queue in memory C. Grafana Mimir 3.2.2 Remote write into a horizontally scaled, multi-tenant store on object storage Made for many tenants, with per-tenant limits. Same object storage model as Thanos AGPL-3.0, which a partner's lawyers have to clear before it runs inside a service they sell. Mimir authenticates nobody: it trusts the X-Scope-OrgID header and its docs require an authenticating proxy in front. A lot of moving parts for two sites, even in monolithic mode D. VictoriaMetrics v1.154.1 Remote write into VictoriaMetrics, single node or cluster Apache-2.0, small, fast, easy to run Keeps its data on local disks; object storage only holds backups (vmbackup). Long-term storage would live on the Paris disks. Downsampling is an Enterprise feature (docs at v1.154.1, "Downsampling")

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Both sites use Thanos, in different ways: Receive for Finland, a sidecar for Paris, with one Query over both and the bucket.

Finland gets Receive because it's the only option where the data leaves the site as it's produced and nothing in Paris has to reach into Finland. The sidecar fails on both counts here. A site that lives for two hours never cuts a block, and a querier in Paris would need a door into Finland that disappears with the site anyway.

Paris gets a sidecar, not remote write, because Paris is the permanent site and its Prometheus should keep working when Receive is down. Receive runs on the Paris CPU worker, which is powered off most of the time to save money. Remote write from Paris would leave its own Prometheus retrying into nothing for days.

Receive authenticates the Finland site with mutual TLS and takes the tenant from the certificate's common name (--receive.tenant-certificate-field=commonName). The Finland site can only write as fin, and each site gets its own TSDB and its own blocks in the bucket. Mimir would need a separate proxy to do what this flag does.

The H200 run on 22 October confirmed it. The Finland series were in the Paris Query about 4 seconds after the Finland Prometheus was Ready. In about half an hour the site sent 4,676,183 samples, none failed or retried. The series were still served from Paris after the site was deleted.

What would change the answer:

  • A partner whose sites are all permanent, with a reliable WAN: a sidecar on every site, store gateways reading the bucket, and one Query fanning out. Nothing extra sits in the write path, and an outage between sites delays queries without losing data. That is how Paris runs here.
  • Thousands of GPUs across many clusters writing to one place: Receive needs a hashring, a replication factor of 3 and per-tenant limits. At 40 to 51 DCGM series per GPU, measured on the L4 and the H200s, 10,000 GPUs make about half a million DCGM series before pod-label churn. At that size Mimir's tenant limits and query sharding deserve a fresh look, if the AGPL is acceptable.
  • No object storage at all: VictoriaMetrics on local disks is simpler than any of these, if the partner can do without downsampling or buys Enterprise.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One PromQL endpoint for every GPU of both sites, and the Finland metrics stay queryable after the site is deleted: from Receive for 3 days, then from the bucket through the store gateway.
  • A CA lives in the Paris cluster. A Job generates it and the certificates once, and they never go into Git. Adding a site means a new client certificate, and its common name becomes the tenant.
  • One Receive, no hashring: a single point of failure in the write path. If it's down while the Finland site runs, the Finland Prometheus keeps its WAL and retries. If the outage outlasts the WAL, those samples are lost.
  • The compactor must be the only one writing to the bucket. One replica here, and it stays that way.
  • Rebuild order. kube-prometheus-stack 91.4.1 only accepts the sidecar's bucket secret as existingSecret, and drops optional (templates/prometheus/prometheus.yaml). So the Paris Prometheus can't start without that Secret. Garage used to create it at wave 5, after this chart's wave 0, so a Paris site rebuilt from nothing would have held at wave 0. Now the base Application objstore-credentials writes it at wave -1, and Garage's wave 5 Job imports that key (findings).
  • MIG changes what the GPU rules count. Each MIG instance gets its own DCGM series, labelled GPU_I_ID, and DCGM_FI_DEV_GPU_UTIL isn't reported for MIG instances. The recording rule and the dashboard don't handle that yet: after the split they count GPUs wrong, as the use case 6 page shows. Grouping by GPU_I_ID and counting GPUs from a field every instance reports is the next change.
  • What this PoC can't show:
  • replication or a hashring, with one Receive and one site writing to it
  • cardinality beyond three GPUs: the 1,000 and 10,000 GPU figures are an extrapolation from measured per-GPU counts, not a load test
  • downsampling on real data before about two days of Paris uploads have built up (shown on SIMULATED blocks instead)
  • the Finland site's last block in the bucket after the H200 run, which I haven't listed yet

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• Local end to end of the Finland write path, using Thanos v0.42.4 and Prometheus 3.14.0. The certificate Job's sign step runs as written, and samples arrive as tenant_id="fin" with site="fin". A client without a certificate is refused at the TLS handshake, and so is a CN=fin certificate from another CA.
  • Checks of the manifests without a GPU:
  • all 37 Thanos flags exist in v0.42.4
  • kube-prometheus-stack renders for both sites with the overlays
  • every object passes a server-side dry run in Paris
  • promtool tests pass, and a deliberately broken rule fails them
  • Source, at the pinned versions: cmd/thanos/receive.go, pkg/tenancy/tenancy.go and pkg/compact/downsample/downsample.go at Thanos v0.42.4; tsdb/head.go at Prometheus v3.14.0; pkg/prometheus/server/statefulset.go at prometheus-operator v0.94.0; Mimir's "Authentication and authorization" page at mimir-3.2.2; VictoriaMetrics' README at v1.154.1.
  • The hub in Paris, 21 October:
  • deduplication merges fin-sim's two replicas
  • Receive accepts fin-sim's writes
  • the Paris sidecar has uploaded 14 blocks with no failures
  • port 30291 doesn't answer from my laptop
  • The bucket, 21 October:
  • the compactor's 5 minute blocks from SIMULATED backfill
  • Receive's 12 s fin-sim block flushed at a power-off
  • A CPU-only test of the Finland site, 21 October:
  • while it ran: the Finland series in the Paris Query as tenant_id="fin", 0 failed samples
  • after deletion: still there 16 minutes after the site was deleted
  • The H200 run, 22 October:
  • whole GPUs: 2x H200 in the Paris Query, 40 DCGM series each
  • after the MIG split and its labels: 20 series per MIG instance, 11 for the split device
  • after deletion: last sample 26 s before the deletion, 4,676,183 samples sent, 0 failed

docs.title: ADR 0010: VM tenants, KubeVirt on the same cluster, with KVM
docs.text: Status: accepted Scope: VM tenants, Paris CPU pool (use case 7). Decided after the first VM boot, 21 October 2026.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Some of Nordhaven's tenants can't move to containers yet: they ship a whole operating system image, or a licensed appliance, or software that expects to own a kernel. Nordhaven still wants to sell them capacity from the same fleet and run that fleet with the same people and tools as the container tenants.

There are two decisions here. Where those VMs run, and, for this PoC, whether they run on hardware virtualisation or on software emulation. The second one I could settle without renting anything: the Paris CPU worker, a Scaleway POP2-8C-32G, exposes /dev/kvm with AMD SVM (node facts).

docs.title: Options considered
docs.text:
Where the VMs run:

Option What it is For Nordhaven Against, for Nordhaven A. KubeVirt on the same clusters VMs as Kubernetes objects, each one a QEMU/KVM process inside a virt-launcher pod One scheduler, one quota system, one GitOps flow and one monitoring stack for both kinds of tenant. Spare CPU capacity goes to whichever kind needs it. The GPU Operator already knows how to prepare a node for VM passthrough or vGPU Kubernetes now carries tenants' operating systems, so a cluster upgrade can restart their VMs unless live migration works. Some VM features (snapshots, disk import) need extra components, CDI first. Operators have to understand both worlds B. A separate IaaS for VM tenants OpenStack, or the provider's own VMs, on a separate pool of hosts The usual model for VM tenants, with mature VM features. A Kubernetes upgrade can't touch a VM Two control planes, two quota systems and two on-call rotations. Capacity is split ahead of time and can't flow between the pools. GPUs would be split the same way, which is the most expensive place to waste capacity

How this PoC runs them:

Option For Against KVM (useEmulation: false) What production would use. The guest sees real hardware virtualisation Needs /dev/kvm on the node: bare metal, or a cloud VM with nested virtualisation exposed Emulation (useEmulation: true) Runs anywhere, including KIND on a laptop QEMU's software CPU is many times slower. Fine for testing manifests; it says nothing about real VM performance

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
KubeVirt on the same clusters, with KVM.

For Nordhaven, the deciding argument is the GPUs. A VM tenant who later wants a GPU gets one from the same pool as everyone else, through the GPU Operator's sandbox mode, rather than from a pool sized months in advance for VM tenants only. Running one control plane is the second argument: the quota, the GitOps flow and the dashboards I already built for container tenants cover the VM tenant with no second system.

KVM costs nothing extra here, because the CPU worker has it. I didn't need emulation, so nothing in use case 7 is simulated.

The first boot on 21 October bore it out: the VM was Running 25 seconds after it was created, the guest reported kvm and booted in 20.2 seconds, and it kept running on the CPU worker while a training job used the L4 on another node (use case 7 page).

What would change the answer:

  • A partner whose VM business is large and runs on its own (many VM-only tenants, VM features like snapshots and live migration of every VM during every upgrade): a mature IaaS next to Kubernetes, and KubeVirt only for the occasional VM inside a container tenant's cluster.
  • GPU passthrough to VMs. It needs bare metal, IOMMU on in the firmware and on the kernel command line (amd_iommu=on / intel_iommu=on), and a node that runs either containers, passthrough VMs or vGPU VMs, never a mix (GPU Operator 26.7 docs, "GPU Operator with KubeVirt"). A PCI-passthrough GPU can't be live-migrated (KubeVirt user guide, "Live migration"). vGPU can be, behind the VGPULiveMigration gate, which is Alpha since KubeVirt v1.9.0. A partner planning GPU VMs plans node pools by workload type. That doesn't change the decision; it changes how the fleet is labelled.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• One more operator on each cluster that has VM tenants. Here it runs on the CPU worker. The release manifest pins virt-operator to control-plane nodes, so a patch moves it, and the KubeVirt resource places virt-api and virt-controller.
  • Every KubeVirt image is pinned by digest, and a bump has to update all of them. The release manifest names images by tag only. A digest on virt-operator's own image doesn't reach the components it deploys: it builds each one as <registry>/<name>:<KUBEVIRT_VERSION>, unless that component's *_IMAGE env var gives a full reference. So pin-images.yaml sets thirteen digests: the operator, virt-api, virt-controller, virt-handler, virt-launcher, the export proxy and server, the synchronization controller, libguestfs, pr-helper, sidecar-shim, and the two virt-template components. The virt-template components follow their own releases, at v0.2.3 for KubeVirt v1.9.1, from a manifest the operator embeds. They deploy by default, because their Template gate is Beta and Beta gates are on unless disabled. A first version of this ADR said the gate was off and left them unpinned; the first deployment in Paris showed them running from their tags. make kubevirt-check fails on any reference left on a bare tag, but it can only check the env vars it knows about. A KubeVirt bump has to diff the operator's *_IMAGE constants in pkg/virt-operator/util/config.go, and then look at what actually runs (make kubevirt-capture lists every pod's image).
  • A VM's cost counts against its tenant's ResourceQuota through its virt-launcher pod, which requests the guest's memory plus an overhead. For a 2 GiB guest the quota counted 1005m CPU and 2349 Mi of memory, about 15% more than the guest's memory. Tenants have to size quotas for that.
  • With one CPU worker there's nowhere to live-migrate to, so the VM sets evictionStrategy: None and stops when the worker is drained. A real VM pool needs at least two nodes, and RWX storage or migratable disks, before it can promise anything across maintenance.
  • What this PoC can't show:
  • GPU passthrough, which needs a bare-metal GPU node; both GPU types rented here are cloud VMs
  • live migration, with one worker
  • disk import and snapshots, because CDI isn't installed

docs.title: Evidence
docs.text:
• /dev/kvm and AMD SVM on the CPU worker: cpu-worker-facts.txt, captured 2026-10-20 by scripts/par/cpu-up.sh.
  • KubeVirt 1.9 supports Kubernetes 1.34 to 1.36 (kubevirt/sig-release, releases/k8s-support-matrix.md).
  • Placement: pkg/virt-operator/resource/placement/placement.go and pkg/virt-operator/resource/generate/components/deployments.go at KubeVirt v1.9.1.
  • Image references: getConfig and getTag in pkg/virt-operator/util/config.go, and the *_IMAGE fallbacks in components/deployments.go and components/daemonsets.go, at v1.9.1. Digests come from quay.io's registry API for tag v1.9.1 (2026-10-20) and v0.2.3 (virt-template, 2026-10-21), checked against its tag API.
